Une semaine s’est écoulée depuis que la: A week has passed since Russia invaded Ukraine once again and came up against Ukrainian forces, which have been putting up courageous resistance ever since. While the context of this invasion has its origins in the breakup of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, today, amid the bombings and gunfire, Ukraine is already suffering the significant humanitarian and geopolitical repercussions of this war.
« Ma ville natale de Tchernihiv a beauco: “My hometown of Chernihiv has suffered a great deal. We heard alarms every 30 minutes, and rockets were falling on houses and historic buildings. While the negotiations were taking place, the rockets kept flying, one after another,” says Veronika Rybak from Montréal. Rybak is a former Ukrainian journalist and political commentator who has lived in Canada for three years. A large number of Ukrainian women and children are hiding in cellars and bomb shelters, while the men organize and carry out the country’s defence, managing to hold back the enemy’s overwhelming forces. More than a million Ukrainians have fled their country. “The army and civilians are defending the cities and pushing back the occupiers, but additional military aid is needed,” adds Ms. Rybak.
Veronika Rybak, journaliste et commentat: Veronika Rybak, journalist and political commentator.
En Ukraine, on interroge plusieurs témoi: In Ukraine, we spoke with several witnesses who want the whole world to know: the war did not begin last week, it began in 2014. Veronika Rybak also believes that to understand this invasion, we need to look a little at history. “In 2013, the president of the Russian Federation could dictate his laws and rules on Ukrainian territory,” the journalist explains. “At the time, the president of Ukraine was Viktor Yanukovych. He reported his every move to Vladimir Putin. Yanukovych’s party created a solid network of parties, where everything was directed from the top, even in the villages,” she tells us. “Then, when the opportunity came to join the European Union (EU), of course Yanukovych refused, because his neighbour, Putin himself, didn’t want it. He didn’t want to be associated with a member of the EU,” Ms. Rybak continues. When President Yanukovych refused to join the EU in 2013, more than 80 people went to Maidan, in downtown Kyiv, to protest. They were brutalized there before being driven from the square.
C’est de cet incident qu’est née la révo: From this incident came the Ukrainian revolution of 2013-2014, dubbed Euromaidan. The goals of the revolution later evolved, aiming not only at joining the EU but also at removing Ukraine’s president from power. Panicked, Viktor Yanukovych fled to the Russian Federation, asking for Putin’s protection, the political analyst tells us. According to her, this situation caused the Kremlin to lose control. The Russian army moved into Sevastopol, in Crimea, which was then part of Ukrainian territory. Fearing obstacles, Putin held an illegal referendum in Crimea to bring the peninsula under Russian control. It was the first time since the Second World War that a European state had annexed part of the territory of another European state. Protests broke out in several Ukrainian cities. Despite this, Putin decided to send troops into the Luhansk and Donetsk regions, under the pretext of “helping Ukraine” – a military operation that has now lasted eight years. Crimea is still under Russian control. “Ukraine is a buffer zone with Europe, and if Ukraine is not under Russia’s control, Russia will surely become vulnerable to Europe,” Ms. Rybak sums up.
Plusieurs experts affirment que, d’un po: Several experts say that, from a geopolitical point of view, the war between Ukraine and Russia was inevitable. Its outbreak was only a matter of time. In his book The Grand Chessboard, American political scientist Zbigniew Brzezinski analyzes the consequences of the collapse of the USSR and writes that Ukraine’s departure was the most painful event for Moscow. Over time, it became clear that the Kremlin would never come to terms with such a loss and was only waiting for an opportunity to take the country back. During its three decades of independence, Ukraine has tried to chart its own course as a sovereign state while seeking closer ties with the West, notably the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). But the president of the Russian Federation views NATO’s eastward expansion as a threat to his country’s territorial integrity.
L’Ukraine n’est pas membre de l’OTAN, et: Ukraine is not a member of NATO, and Russia has repeatedly asked for a promise that Ukraine will never join. In 2014, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine turned the Donbas region into a battlefield. According to statements by British military leaders and American investigators, Russian military forces were built up along the border with Ukraine in late 2021. It was already clear at that point that Moscow was preparing for a large-scale invasion of Ukraine.
<strong>Les intérêts de la Russie en Ukr: Russia’s interests in Ukraine from a historical perspective
Roman Serbyn est professeur émérite d’hi: Roman Serbyn is professor emeritus of Russian and Eastern European history at the Université du Québec à Montréal and a specialist on Ukraine. He believes that Putin is continuing the policy of Joseph Stalin, the former Soviet leader, namely the integration of Ukraine into the Russian state. “Stalin wanted to turn the Soviet Union into a Russian state. He suppressed the Ukrainian renaissance; there was the Holodomor (the great famine) in Ukraine, and the destruction of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church and the intelligentsia,” the professor says. “When Ukraine was conquered by the Bolsheviks (the Russian army), it was given the status of a Ukrainian socialist republic. That means it did not become a state that made its own laws, but one that was subject to higher powers,” says Mr. Serbyn.
Il pense que Poutine veut reconstituer l: He thinks Putin wants to rebuild the Soviet empire. “According to Putin’s controversial essay On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians, published on July 12, 2021, the Ukrainian language never existed, any more than the Ukrainian state did,” the professor explains. “The essay shows that the goal of this war is the conquest of Kyiv and a change of government that would gradually realign Ukraine with the wholly Russian nation,” he says. Mr. Serbyn believes that if Ukraine remains a sovereign state, it weakens Russia. “Putin said he wanted NATO to withdraw not only from Ukraine, but also from the republics that belonged to the Soviet Union,” he adds. In short, the Ukraine specialist maintains that Putin wants to abolish Ukraine as an independent state and a distinct ethnic group, and that if the Russian president manages to take control of Ukraine, which has the largest area of the former Soviet republics, Russia will become more powerful. “After Ukraine is integrated, it will be easier to integrate other republics,” he suggests. “And then, it changes the relationships at the geopolitical level.”
Inga Kononenko, analyste en matière d’in: Inga Kononenko, an analyst of international human rights institutions and policies, worked for the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) during the parliamentary and presidential elections in Ukraine. She believes that, according to the Kremlin’s current rhetoric, the very existence of Ukraine as an independent state is unthinkable. “In their logic, Ukraine can only exist as a colony of Russia. Vladimir Putin made it clear that he would never allow Ukraine to become ‘anti-Russian’ and that he would continue to oppose the expansion of Western influence in Ukraine,” says Ms. Kononenko. She observes that as Ukraine moves forward and develops its own identity and a modern perception of itself, Russia is seeking to reclaim a role by mixing in various ideologies, including the Soviet ideology of the 20th century. The human rights specialist believes that by occupying Crimea, Russia has strengthened its control over the Black Sea by establishing a larger and more modern military presence on the peninsula.
Mercredi soir, de l’autre côté de l’Atla: On Wednesday evening, from across the Atlantic, we spoke with Andriy Titok, a journalist who covers military affairs for the National Public Broadcasting Company of Ukraine (UA:PBC). He reports that the Russian occupying forces are violating international humanitarian law by looting and killing local populations. “The morale of the occupying army is extremely low,” he tells us by phone from the city of Chernihiv. He notes that the United States and its allies have taken retaliatory measures against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, but believes this is not enough. “We all understand that if they get actively involved in this conflict, there will be a world war. But Ukraine really needs military aid today,” he says. He points out that eight years ago, when it was plain to see that Russia had invaded Ukraine, annexed Crimea and set off a war in the Donbas region, the international community had been too accommodating toward Vladimir Putin.
« Les politiciens canadiens, américains: “Canadian, American and European politicians tried to please Putin. But we all know the lessons to be learned from 1938-1939, when Europeans also flattered the aggressor Hitler,” argues the journalist who covers military affairs. Titok believes that the recent sanctions imposed on Russia by Western countries should have come sooner. Professor Roman Serbyn agrees, saying these sanctions should have been imposed at the very start of the invasion, in 2014. On February 26, Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union <l1>decided</l1> to block certain Russian banks’ access to the SWIFT global payment system in order to shake Russia’s economy and finances. But according to Mr. Serbyn, this measure is insufficient and will take too long to have an effect. “It will take weeks before the SWIFT system is shut off, and in the meantime, Ukrainians will be killed or will live under occupation,” says the professor. “Ukraine did not ask Americans and Canadians to go to war for Ukraine. It asked for military aid and weapons. Over there, the army advances with weapons, but they [Western leaders] talk about ‘sanctions.’ Putin is going to keep attacking, and we are going to impose sanctions and empty out their embassies. Isn’t that an incentive for Putin?” Mr. Serbyn continues. On February 27, 2022, <l2>NATO</l2> said that Belgium, Canada, the Czech Republic, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Great Britain and the United States had already sent, or were in the process of approving, major deliveries of military equipment to Ukraine, along with several million dollars, while other member countries would provide humanitarian aid by taking in refugees.
Les intervenants rencontrés dans le cadr: The people interviewed for this report say that as Ukraine pushed to join NATO and the EU, it asserted its sovereignty and forged a modern image for itself. However, tensions have intensified, particularly since Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and took control of Donetsk and Luhansk, regions in southeastern Ukraine. Andriy Titok, a journalist in Ukraine, is calling on Canadians to pressure their governments to open a second front and put pressure on the Kremlin. Veronika Rybak wants the world to understand that Ukraine is defending its territorial integrity and that this is what keeps the Kremlin from invading other European countries. “The world must not stay silent,” she says. “It’s probably the only thing that can stop Russia. Every small gesture we make for Ukraine is a drop that helps form a vast ocean of aid.”
« Un cessez-le-feu est toujours judicieu: “A ceasefire is always a good idea,” says Inga Kononenko. “But the problem is that Russia made the first moves, and it’s clear that it wants to buy time.” “Another problem for Ukraine is that Belarus has officially entered the war,” the analyst adds. “With their referendum, they have the power to support Russia.” And on Ukraine’s side? “The fact that it has shown its willingness to take part in negotiations allows it to expect more on the international front and to push for measures like a no-fly zone; something that still hasn’t been done and that is really needed to counter what we are witnessing today in Ukrainian cities,” she concludes.
<strong>Quels sont les discours véhiculé: What narratives is the Kremlin putting forward?
La Russie a affirmé à plusieurs reprises: Russia has repeatedly claimed that it launched its military intervention in order to protect, “demilitarize and denazify Ukraine.” “The aim of this operation is to protect people who, for eight years, have been subjected to bullying and genocide by the Kyiv regime,” Vladimir Putin said in a televised address. On March 1, 2022, the Russian embassy in Canada published a statement along the same lines. It claims that crimes against humanity and violations of international humanitarian law are being committed by neo-Nazi groups such as the Azov Regiment and the Right Sector party. “The Russian army is not fighting Ukraine or Ukrainians. The tasks of ridding Ukraine of Nazism and demilitarizing it will be accomplished,” the statement reads. Many say they are baffled by the idea that Putin wants to denazify Ukraine, a country whose president, Volodymyr Zelensky, is Jewish. Does this mean Russia wants to protect the Jews, Roma, international students and LGBTQ communities living in Ukraine? In the next part of our series on Ukraine, we will explore this question further.
